issues.legal_issue: A landlord who obtained an eviction order may support its operative result in a tenant’s revision by relying on an eviction ground rejected below, without filing a revision of the landlord’s own, if the landlord seeks only to sustain that result.
material_facts: The landlord obtained an eviction order on one ground, while the claim on another ground was rejected by the appellate authority.
The tenant filed a revision challenging the eviction order; the landlord did not file a revision but argued that the order could also be sustained on the rejected ground.
The landlord sought to uphold the eviction order, not to obtain a more beneficial or larger order.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could consider the landlord’s alternative ground and sustain the eviction order on it, even though the landlord had not filed a revision of its own.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965 gives the revisional court broad authority to examine the legality, regularity, and propriety of the subordinate authority’s order, including parts of it. A respondent who succeeded in the operative result is not aggrieved by that result merely because a finding went against it, and may support the result on another ground; a party seeking a larger or more beneficial result must bring its own revision. The Court relied on Shankar Ramchandra Abhyankar v. Krishnaji Dattatraya Bapat, Major S.S. Khanna v. Brig. F.J. Dhillon, Babulal Nagar v. Shree Synthetics Ltd., Hukumchand Mills Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Gangabai v. Vijay Kumar, Seetaram v. Ramabai, Gaddem Chinna Venkata Rao v. Koralla Satyanarayanamurthy, and K. Venkataramani v. S. Aravamuthan.

predicates.tenant_revision_in_rent_control_proceedi: The tenant brought a revision challenging an eviction order in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.landlord_succeeded_in_operative_eviction: The landlord obtained an operative eviction order, although one or more grounds it had advanced were rejected.
predicates.landlord_seeks_only_to_sustain_order: The landlord asks only that the existing operative result be upheld and does not seek a larger or more beneficial order.
predicates.adverse_finding_rejected_alternative_gro: The lower authority rejected an alternative ground on which the landlord says the operative eviction result can also be sustained.

issues.definition: When a tenant brings a revision, the landlord has an operative eviction order in its favour, the landlord seeks only to sustain that result, and an alternative ground was rejected below, the landlord may rely on that ground without bringing its own revision.

issues.legal_issue: A subtenant who acquires the landlord’s full ownership interest and reversion in the premises ceases to hold the sublet portion as a subtenant by merger and may seek eviction for additional personal accommodation while occupying part of the building as owner-landlord.
material_facts: The premises were one building let to the tenant under a single tenancy, although local numbering divided it into separate portions.
The tenant had sublet one portion to the person who later purchased the entire property, including the reversion in the tenant’s premises.
After the purchase, the purchaser occupied the sublet portion and sought the remaining portion for personal use as additional accommodation.
The sale deed was not challenged, and there was no indication that the parties intended to prevent the subtenancy from merging into the purchaser’s ownership.
issues.conclusion: The subtenancy ended by merger when the subtenant acquired full ownership and the reversion; the purchaser became the owner-landlord and could rely on the additional-accommodation ground for eviction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11(8) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965 allows a landlord occupying part of a building to seek the remaining part for personal use as additional accommodation. Sections 111(d) and 109 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 govern merger of the lesser leasehold interest into the greater ownership interest and the rights of a transferee of the lessor’s interest. Merger depends substantially on intention and circumstances, with a presumption against merger where it would disadvantage a party; here the acquired ownership and reversion were complete, and the subtenancy could not coexist with that greater estate. Section 109 permits transfer of part of the reversion and statutory attornment without the tenant’s consent. The Court relied on Mohar Singh v. Devi Charan, B.P. Pathak v. Dr. Riyazuddin, and Sardarilal v. Narayanlal.

rule.if: rent_control_additional_accommodation_proceeding and landlord_occupies_part_of_building and landlord_requires_remaining_part_for_personal_use and landlord_held_occupied_part_as_subtenant and landlord_acquired_full_ownership_and_reversion

predicates.rent_control_additional_accommodation_pr: The proceeding seeks eviction in a rent-control matter on the basis that an occupying landlord needs additional accommodation for personal use.
predicates.landlord_occupies_part_of_building: The landlord occupies only part of the building and a tenant occupies another part.
predicates.landlord_requires_remaining_part_for_per: The landlord requires the tenant-occupied part for the landlord’s personal use as additional accommodation.
predicates.landlord_held_occupied_part_as_subtenant: The landlord’s occupation of the part already occupied by the landlord originated as a subtenancy under the tenant.
predicates.landlord_acquired_full_ownership_and_rev: The landlord acquired the full ownership interest, including the reversion, in the premises.

issues.definition: When an additional-accommodation eviction proceeding involves an owner-landlord occupying part of a building, needing the remaining part for personal use, having originally occupied the first part as a subtenant, and acquiring full ownership and the reversion, the subtenancy ends by merger and the owner-landlord may seek eviction.
